items.title: neuralopt
items.text: neuralopt tests a compact transformer policy for bounded numerical optimization alongside a deliberately restricted interval certificate system. Start with the repository README, then read the mathematical specification and limitations before using certified mode.

items.title: Held-out quadratic smoke result
items.text:
On 15 November 2026, the 100-step demo checkpoint was evaluated on three held-out four-dimensional quadratic instances (seed 42, budget 100). Median final objective was 13.0525 for the trained policy, 195.745 for random policy weights, and 2.14e-12 for SciPy L-BFGS-B with analytic JAX gradients. Median end-to-end times were 0.635 s, 0.652 s, and 0.0329 s respectively on the onboarding CPU environment. Compilation was included.

The trained policy improved on random initialization but lost decisively to the conventional baseline. This rejects H2 for this small task distribution and checkpoint. Three instances are a smoke check, not statistical evidence for H1. Raw measurements are in results/heldout-smoke.json; training loss fell from 0.260531 to 0.00994861 in 100 updates (about 12 seconds).

items.title: Benchmark protocol
items.text:
Machine-readable rows must separate objective calls, gradient calls, derivative products, compilation, warm execution, loading, and total time. Compilation is not silently amortized. Comparisons are paired by instance and seed and report medians, intervals, success, and anytime regret. Objective wrappers enforce the requested budget even when a third-party solver would finish an over-budget line search. Regret is null, rather than zero, when a task has no known optimum. All baselines return the tracked best finite in-budget observation. Nonfinite samples cannot replace a valid incumbent; a run with no finite observation fails explicitly instead of emitting a misleading NaN result. Solver state remains NumPy-compatible, but objective and gradient callbacks receive JAX arrays in the problem's declared dtype. Benchmarks therefore support the same array-specific objective operations as native NeuralOpt inference.

The current v0.2 artifact is only a smoke experiment. A fixed normalized-gradient control beats v0.1.0 on every recorded family; for example, its final values are 0.0286 versus 0.4685 (isotropic), 24.61 versus 293.0 (ill-conditioned), and 5.918 versus 71.46 (rotated). These are single instances and do not support a superiority claim. SciPy, Adam, Optimistix, differential evolution, quasi-random search, trained MLP, and BBOB performance profiles remain an uncompleted M4 milestone.

items.title: Development performance profile
items.text:
Single-run CPU timings from the development environment (November 2026) are diagnostic, not publication benchmarks. Compiling the policy, objective, and gradient once per run reduced warm learned-inference cost as follows:

Dimension Before Current Evaluations 4 7.80 ms/eval 1.18 ms/eval 100 32 8.32 ms/eval 1.70 ms/eval 100

Cold 100-evaluation runs remain about 1.1--1.2 seconds because JAX compilation dominates. Warm execution still synchronizes once per candidate and uses a Python optimization loop; batching or a compiled loop is the next runtime bottleneck. Independently, the measured 0--4.1% v0.1 acceptance rate remains a larger algorithmic efficiency problem than kernel dispatch.

items.title: Certified scheduling
items.text:
Certification now exposes deterministic lower-bound or width region priority, widest or round-robin legal splitting, and callbacks for learned ranking and split selection. Callbacks affect scheduling only: interval lower bounds, incumbents, pruning, and termination remain native and rigorous under the stated floating-point assumptions. Default lower-bound scheduling reads the global bound from the scheduling heap root. Alternative and learned priorities maintain a second lower-bound heap with lazy deletion, avoiding a full active-set scan after every processed node.

Every terminal pruned box is serialized. Independent replay re-evaluates each interval bound, checks that boxes lie inside the original domain, compares total leaf and domain volume, rejects positive-volume overlap, and checks the final gap. Partition replay follows shared bisection boundaries recursively, avoiding quadratic all-pairs overlap checks. This closes the v0.1.0 verifier's domain-accounting omission while remaining practical for thousands of leaves.

On the dependency-stress expression x[0] - x[0], 8,191 processed nodes and 8,192 retained leaves took about 0.89 seconds for search and 0.68 seconds for replay after the current fixes. Scaling from 2,048 to 16,384 leaves was close to linear. Search time is dominated by interval-expression evaluation and Interval object validation; replay is dominated by recursive partition reconstruction, followed by re-evaluating every retained interval bound.

No learned certification policy has yet been trained or benchmarked. Therefore there is no supported node-count or wall-time speedup claim.

items.title: Equations and gradient path
items.text:
The transformer predicts A = diag(d) + U U^T, where d is produced by a softplus plus 1e-4. Overdamped training uses

\[z_{n+1}=z_n-hA abla U(z_n)+\sqrt{2Th}\,(D^{1/2}\xi+U\eta),\]

with the bounded transformed potential U(z) = f(x(z)) - T log|dx/dz|. BAOAB uses the same factor as a mass matrix, its Woodbury inverse in the drift, and exact Ornstein--Uhlenbeck momentum covariance T(1-exp(-2 gamma h)) M. Explicit PRNG keys make trajectories reproducible and pathwise differentiation carries gradients through both drift geometry and noise scale. The BAOAB rollout also samples its initial momentum from N(0, T M) using the first predicted mass, matching the inference transition rather than beginning from an artificial zero-momentum state.

The weak Fokker--Planck term compares the conditional expected one-step change of phi(z)=mean(z^2) with

\[L\phi=b^T abla\phi+ frac12\operatorname{tr}(a abla^2\phi), \qquad a=2TA.\]

Mobility is frozen only within an episode. Updating it from trajectory history makes the optimizer nonstationary. Euler and BAOAB retain finite-step bias; the experiment makes no exact Gibbs or finite-step stationarity claim. The quadratic Gaussian noise contribution is evaluated analytically rather than sampled, avoiding a variance term that would reward shrinking mobility.

items.title: Protocol
items.text:
• Model: width 16, four heads, rank two, one transformer layer.
  • Training: 36 Adam updates at 3e-4, global gradient clipping, seed 17.
  • Trajectory: six episodes, two integration steps per episode, horizons 2/4/6, step size 0.008, temperature 0.5.
  • Training set: shifted, rotated, condition-10 to condition-1000 quadratics, Rastrigin, Ackley, and Rosenbrock in dimensions two through four.
  • Held out: ten paired instances spanning rotated and ill-conditioned quadratics, Rosenbrock, Ackley, and Rastrigin in unseen dimensions three to six and seeds 40/41.
  • Primary evaluation: objective budget 80 and temperature 0.5. Paired percentile bootstrap intervals use 10,000 resamples.
  • Transfer evaluation: temperatures 0.25/1.0 and budgets 40/120 on four held-out instances. These small four-instance intervals are descriptive.

The machine-readable record is results/geometry-training-v0.4.0.json. The three portable checkpoints are in artifacts/neuralopt-v0.4.0-*.npz. Reproduce with uv run python scripts/run_geometry_training_v0_4.py; use --reuse-checkpoints to repeat evaluation without retraining.

items.title: Primary held-out results
items.text:
Differences are paired mean log1p(regret) relative to identity; negative is better. All variants used the same objective budgets. Overdamped runs used 78 gradient evaluations and 52 integration steps; BAOAB used 75 and 30.

Integrator and geometry Mean log regret Difference vs identity (95% CI) Wins/10 Overdamped identity 2.854 0.000 -- Overdamped fixed diagonal 2.804 -0.050 [-0.282, 0.143] 3 Overdamped untrained transformer 2.661 -0.193 [-0.553, 0.075] 5 Overdamped regret trained 2.678 -0.177 [-0.452, 0.056] 6 Overdamped regret + FP 2.630 -0.224 [-0.552, 0.039] 6 BAOAB identity 1.712 0.000 -- BAOAB fixed diagonal 1.272 -0.441 [-0.878, -0.078] 6 BAOAB untrained transformer 1.460 -0.253 [-0.790, 0.091] 4 BAOAB regret trained 1.685 -0.028 [-0.259, 0.207] 3 BAOAB transferred regret + FP 1.465 -0.247 [-0.752, 0.072] 4

The direct paired FP-minus-regret comparison is -0.048 with 95% interval [-0.105, -0.006] for overdamped dynamics (5/10 wins). This is evidence on the small prespecified held-out set, not a universal advantage. For BAOAB transfer the difference is -0.220 [-0.570, 0.022], so no improvement is established.

At unseen temperatures and budgets the overdamped FP-minus-regret point estimate remained negative in all four settings, but every four-instance interval touched or crossed zero. At budget 40, transferred FP geometry was worse for BAOAB at both temperatures (+0.377 at 0.25 and +0.357 at 1.0). The simple fixed diagonal remains the strongest supported BAOAB result.

Training took 22.9 seconds for overdamped regret, 28.9 seconds for BAOAB regret, and 17.3 seconds for regret plus FP on the recorded CPU run. Median warm inference was about 0.08--0.12 seconds. First-call timings in the shared process are cache- and order-sensitive and are retained in the artifact rather than interpreted as isolated compilation measurements.

items.title: Correctness and remaining gaps
items.text:
Tests verify positive diagonals, diagonal-plus-low-rank covariance, exact OU fluctuation--dissipation scaling, reproducibility, Gaussian moments, finite nonzero gradients into both geometry heads, weak generator identities, and nonfinite-coordinate rejection. Certification code and independent replay are unchanged.

The experiment is still small: six training tasks, ten primary held-out pairs, one training seed, and no BBOB or scientific inverse problem. FP weighting was not selected on a separate validation sweep, free-energy regularization remains disabled, and objective closures compile independently. Stronger claims require multiple training seeds, larger held-out suites, family-level uncertainty, and batched parameterized task generators.

items.title: Hypothesis experiment plan
items.text:
All comparisons use paired task instances, seeds, dimensions, and evaluation budgets. H1 compares trained and untrained policies on held-out families and dimensions. H2 compares final and anytime regret, evaluations, failures, and wall time against an appropriate classical solver and available faithful learned baselines. H3 compares fixed widest-first branch ordering with model priority while replaying identical certificate rules. H4 records compilation, steady-state policy time, objective calls, parameter count, memory, and training cost. Ablations remove attention, history compression, gradients, low-rank factors, independent proposals, normalization augmentation, pretraining, and learned spatial guidance one factor at a time.

The bundled smoke experiment is insufficient for accepting any hypothesis: it verifies training and serialization on synthetic quadratics only.

items.title: Fokker–Planck foundations
items.text:
For Itô drift b and covariance a = sigma sigma^T, the generator is

\[\mathcal L\varphi=b^T abla\varphi+ frac12\operatorname{tr}(a abla^2\varphi).\]

The forward Kolmogorov equation is the adjoint evolution of this generator. For fixed mobility Langevin dynamics it becomes

\[\partial_t ho= abla\cdot[A( ho abla f+T abla ho)].\]

NeuralOpt implements the small-dimensional generator and Monte Carlo weak-form residual

\[(E[\varphi(X_{n+1})]-E[\varphi(X_n)])/h-E[\mathcal L\varphi(X_n)].\]

Tests validate the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck identity with antithetic noise. This is a diagnostic primitive, not yet a transformer training result. A low residual can coexist with poor optimization regret and is not itself evidence for the central learned-optimizer hypothesis.

The free energy E[f] + T int rho log rho is implemented exactly only for a Gaussian distribution and quadratic objective. The test confirms its minimum at the analytic Gibbs covariance. No arbitrary particle entropy estimator is labelled exact free energy.

Jordan, Kinderlehrer, and Otto (1998) interpret Fokker–Planck evolution as a Wasserstein gradient flow through a minimizing-movement scheme. That continuous-time/variational result is not transferred to finite-step Euler or history-adaptive transformer coefficients.

items.title: Periodic function-space reference experiment
items.text:
There is no infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Function-space probability is formulated relative to a Gaussian reference measure, following Beskos et al. (2011) and Cotter et al. (2013). NeuralOpt's initial periodic reference uses the spectral covariance

\[C_k=(\alpha+|k|^2)^{-p},\qquad p>1/2,\]

and real Fourier synthesis. The compact reconstruction problem minimizes a mesh-normalized L2 data fit plus periodic H1 regularization. Its Fourier solution is analytic, providing an independent refinement reference.

Tests at 32, 64, 128, and 256 points recover the same continuous sine/cosine solution and verify a near-zero discrete gradient. This establishes spectral operator correctness and discretization consistency only. It does not show that the transformer transfers across resolutions, that a learned operator is mesh independent, or that the finite discretization converges as a probability measure in function space.

Dense learned matrices are deliberately absent. A future learned geometry must act relative to the reference covariance through Fourier multipliers or resolution-stable low-rank corrections.

items.title: Generalization
items.text:
Coordinate inputs and gradients are explicitly transformed into normalized box coordinates. If u = 2(x-l)/(h-l)-1, then df/du = (h-l) df/dx / 2. Round-trip behavior is regression tested.

The transformer and the new shared-coordinate MLP baseline have parameter counts independent of objective dimension. The MLP consumes the same coordinate features plus budget and dimension signals, but has no attention; it is smaller than the configured transformer and provides an executable architecture ablation. The bundled checkpoint is transformer-specific. MLP inference therefore requires caller-provided MLP parameters; architecture-specific parameter keys are validated before optimization begins.

Unrotated quadratic tasks retain an elementwise weighted objective with linear storage and evaluation cost. A dense matrix is constructed only when rotation is requested; a 10,000-dimensional regression guards against accidental dense materialization in the default task curriculum.

Only one unseen-dimension smoke result is currently executed: the 12-update regret model worsened an unseen 8D rotated, condition-100 quadratic (164.71 versus 89.41 for v0.1.0). There is not yet enough evidence for interpolation or extrapolation claims. Unseen-family and multi-seed studies are outstanding.

items.title: Gibbs measures and optimization
items.text:
At temperature T, the artificial finite-dimensional Gibbs density is pi_T(x) proportional to exp(-f(x)/T). It is a distribution over feasible states, not an optimizer certificate. Lower temperature concentrates mass near low objective values under suitable assumptions but does not guarantee that a finite trajectory finds a global minimizer.

The logistic bounded transform includes its determinant so fixed-geometry continuous-time dynamics target the mapped bounded Gibbs measure. Euler, BAOAB, and adaptive learned geometry introduce distinct qualifications:

  • Euler–Maruyama and BAOAB have finite-step bias.
  • Episode-frozen learned geometry is fixed only during one episode.
  • Updating geometry from history makes the overall process nonstationary.
  • Changing temperature creates a sequence of targets, not one invariant Gibbs distribution.

Optimization therefore reports the best feasible incumbent separately from the stochastic state. Distributional accuracy, candidate improvement, and incumbent updates are independent measurements.

items.title: Implemented guarantees and restrictions
items.text:
• The fixed metric is positive diagonal plus low rank and is constant during a transition.
  • Momentum covariance and kinetic energy use the same mass convention.
  • Leapfrog uses lax.scan, explicit keys, momentum reversal, and log-space Metropolis correction.
  • Box constraints use a differentiable interior transform with its Jacobian.
  • The unconstrained chain coordinate is retained exactly between transitions; transform clipping is initialization-only.
  • Nonfinite energy and excessive energy error mark a divergent proposal.
  • General nonlinear constraints and host-only objectives fail closed.
  • Adaptive learned metrics have no stationary-HMC claim.

Tests compare Woodbury solves and kinetic energy against dense references, estimate momentum covariance from 20,000 draws, reverse leapfrog trajectories, check reduced drift at smaller step size, test interior feasibility, invalid metrics, and preservation of an exact boundary incumbent. These numerical tests support but do not replace the standard leapfrog reversibility and volume-preservation argument.

items.title: Acceptance diagnosis and smoke experiment
items.text:
scripts/run_hamiltonian_smoke.py evaluates 15 matched instances with a nominal 100-objective-evaluation budget. Direct NeuralOpt proposes 99 candidates; each Hamiltonian variant performs 16 transitions, 32 leapfrog steps, 97 accounted objective evaluations, and 64 gradient evaluations. Results are in results/hamiltonian-smoke-v0.2.0.json.

Variant Transition acceptance Objective improvement Incumbent update Warm runtime Direct NeuralOpt 1.01% 1.01% 1.01% 0.245 s Identity HMC 93.75% 50.0% 31.25% 0.092 s Learned-metric HMC 93.75% 56.25% 18.75% 0.083 s

Identity HMC beats direct final objective on 8/15 paired cases; learned metric beats direct on 9/15 and identity on only 7/15. Median objective ratios versus direct are 0.771 and 0.745, respectively, but objectives from different families must not be pooled as an absolute accuracy statistic. HMC helps rotated quadratics, Rastrigin, and Ackley in this smoke sample, but is substantially worse on isotropic and ill-conditioned quadratics.

Median absolute energy error is 0.114 for identity and 0.162 for learned metric. The first identity-HMC call is about 1.06 s because it compiles the transition; warm timings reuse compilation. High HMC acceptance therefore does not establish better optimization or end-to-end cold-start efficiency.

items.title: Hypothesis status
items.text:
• H1: provisionally supported only on selected families; rejected as a universal statement.
  • H2: not supported; learned geometry does not consistently beat identity.
  • H3: provisionally supported by distinct exploration improvements and a monotone incumbent, but needs larger multimodal studies.
  • H4: unresolved. Warm runtime is favorable under this implementation, but gradient information and cold compilation differ materially.
  • H5: untested. Certification code is unchanged and all replay tests pass, but Hamiltonian incumbents are not yet injected into certified search.

The evidence is a smoke experiment with three seeds, not a powered benchmark. Hamiltonian proposals remain opt-in and must not replace the direct default.

items.title: Hamiltonian related work
items.text:
This review was checked against primary papers and author/reference-manual sources available through 15 November 2026.

Duane et al. (1987) introduced hybrid Monte Carlo; Neal's 2011 handbook chapter established the modern practical account. Hoffman and Gelman's NUTS removes a fixed trajectory-length choice and uses diminishing warm-up adaptation. It is not implemented here because the first experiment isolates fixed integration length and learned mass geometry.

Girolami and Calderhead (2011, JRSS B) introduced Riemannian-manifold HMC, whose position-dependent metric requires nonseparable dynamics, log-determinant terms, and generalized integration. NeuralOpt does not claim RMHMC: its metric is fixed inside each transition. Betancourt's review explains why matching the Euclidean metric to target covariance can improve exploration, but this does not imply that an optimizer-trained preconditioner is automatically a good HMC mass.

Pakman and Paninski (2014, JCGS) developed exact HMC for truncated Gaussian models; Afshar and Domke (2015, NeurIPS) studied reflection/refraction HMC. Those methods motivate correct boundary dynamics. The present implementation instead uses a logistic change of variables and includes its Jacobian, avoiding claims that clipping is reversible or volume preserving.

Levy, Hoffman, and Sohl-Dickstein (2018, ICLR), “Generalizing Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with Neural Networks,” introduced L2HMC, learning reversible volume-preserving transformations. Hoffman et al. (2019), “NeuTra-lizing Bad Geometry in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo,” learned transport maps before HMC. These works learn proposal geometry while preserving explicit sampling corrections. NeuralOpt's history-adaptive transformer metric is more modest and is treated as an optimization heuristic outside the fixed-kernel reference experiment.

Temperature schedules relate the artificial density to simulated annealing (Kirkpatrick, Gelatt, and Vecchi, 1983). Changing beta changes the target; an annealed optimization trajectory is not a sample from one stationary density and does not by itself prove global convergence. Temperature learning remains unimplemented pending evidence that fixed-temperature Hamiltonian candidates justify the added complexity.

items.title: Mathematical facts
items.text:
For fixed inverse temperature beta and mass matrix M, NeuralOpt defines the artificial density pi(x) proportional to exp(-beta f(x)) and Hamiltonian

\[H(x,p)=\beta f(x)+\tfrac12p^T M^{-1}p,\qquad p\sim N(0,M).\]

The implementation uses velocity M^-1 p, not M p. Its learned convention is explicit: the transformer output D + U U^T is the mass matrix. Momentum is sampled as sqrt(D) z + U eta, and Woodbury algebra applies the inverse without forming a dense matrix.

Leapfrog alternates a half momentum update, full position update, and half momentum update. For a fixed separable Hamiltonian it is reversible (with final momentum reversal), symplectic, and volume preserving. The Metropolis decision is evaluated in log space: log(u) < min(0, H_initial - H_proposed). These are the standard constructions described by the Oxford and Washington lecture notes, Hoffman and Gelman, Betancourt, and the Stan reference manual.

Box constraints use x = lo + (hi-lo) sigmoid(z). The unconstrained potential is

\[U(z)=\beta f(x(z))-\log|dx/dz|.\]

The Jacobian term is required for the transformed target. Exact boundary points are not represented by finite z; the optimization incumbent is therefore a separate feasible archive that retains and can return boundary points. The bounded-to-unconstrained conversion, including its numerical clipping, is performed only when a chain is initialized. Every subsequent transition threads the exact accepted unconstrained state; reconstructing and clipping it from the bounded coordinate would change the Markov state and invalidate the kernel.

items.title: Optimization versus sampling
items.text:
Metropolis acceptance means that a phase-space proposal is valid for the fixed target under the documented assumptions. It does not mean the objective improved. An accepted transition may move uphill, while a rejected proposal may still contain a better feasible point worth archiving for optimization. NeuralOpt records transition acceptance, improvement over the exploration state, and best-incumbent updates separately.

The learned metric is fixed during one transition but may change between transitions with optimizer history. This is an adaptive optimization heuristic; no stationary-distribution or detailed-balance claim is made for that adaptive chain. The fixed identity-metric kernel is the reference sampling transition.

items.title: Executable example
items.text:
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from neuralopt import Problem, init_model, minimize
from neuralopt.hamiltonian import HamiltonianConfig

problem = Problem(lambda x: jnp.sum((x - 0.3) ** 2), (-2.0, 2.0), 4)
result = minimize(
    problem,
    params=init_model(jax.random.PRNGKey(0)),
    candidate_method="hamiltonian",
    hamiltonian_metric="identity",
    hamiltonian_config=HamiltonianConfig(step_size=0.03, leapfrog_steps=2),
    max_evaluations=100,
    record_diagnostics=True,
)

items.title: Langevin theory and implementation
items.text:
For fixed positive-definite mobility A, overdamped Langevin dynamics are

\[dX_t=-A\nabla f(X_t)dt+\sqrt{2TA}\,dW_t.\]

Under regularity and integrability assumptions, the continuous-time invariant density is proportional to exp(-f/T). NeuralOpt uses Euler–Maruyama with episode-frozen identity or transformer geometry. The finite-step chain is biased and is not described as an exact Gibbs sampler. Noise is sampled with covariance A = D + U U^T; tests verify covariance, reproducibility, temperature scaling, and Gaussian moments.

For position-dependent mobility, the Itô drift compatible with the Gibbs density contains T div A. mobility_divergence computes this exactly with jacfwd for small-dimensional experiments. It materializes a rank-three Jacobian and is not enabled in the production optimizer. History-adaptive geometry does not inherit a fixed invariant-measure guarantee.

Underdamped dynamics use

\[dX=M^{-1}Pdt,\qquad dP=-\nabla fdt-\gamma Pdt+\sqrt{2\gamma TM}\,dW.\]

The native BAOAB splitting applies half force, half position, exact Ornstein–Uhlenbeck momentum, half position, and half force updates. Its OU step uses exp(-gamma h) and covariance T(1-exp(-2 gamma h))M, satisfying the fluctuation–dissipation relation. BAOAB also has finite-step invariant-measure bias.

Box constraints use the same logistic coordinate transform and Jacobian as HMC. The unconstrained state is threaded between episodes; exact boundary optima are retained by the separate feasible incumbent.

Primary references include Roberts and Tweedie (1996), Girolami and Calderhead (2011), Welling and Teh (2011), and the geometric Langevin literature summarized in hamiltonian-related-work.md.

Diffrax 0.7.2 is an optional sde extra and supplies an independent identity- mobility Euler reference. It is not imported by the base package. Exponax was audited at version 0.2.1 but not added: the present weak-form and periodic-field experiments do not require a density PDE solver, so adding it would not yet have a demonstrated numerical purpose.

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
This v0.2 development prototype has no claim of universal superiority or production maturity. The bundled checkpoint remains the v0.1.0 supervised smoke model. The outcome-trained v0.2 smoke checkpoint failed its unseen-dimension test and is retained only as a negative result. Randomly initialized weights are labelled as such. Learned stopping is not used as a correctness claim.

The optimizer currently requires gradients and supports box constraints only. A JAX-differentiable objective uses compiled automatic differentiation; an explicit gradient keeps objective and gradient callbacks eager so NumPy or other host implementations remain supported. Residuals and nonlinear constraints are represented by the problem type but optimization rejects no constraint violations yet; they are forward-compatible metadata rather than implemented constrained optimization. Full history, curvature sketches, noise models, recurrent ablations, BBOB, MetaBox, ODE inversion, accelerator profiles, and faithful learned-optimizer baselines remain future experiments.

Certification supports an explicit expression language, not JAXPR. Its nextafter backend assumes correctly rounded host operations and libm; it is not IEEE 1788 conformant and cannot establish formal proof across arbitrary platforms. Replay checks retained bounds and geometric domain accounting but does not prove the implementation or hardware. Constraints, division, logarithms, arbitrary powers, interval Newton, Taylor models, and infeasibility proofs are unsupported and fail closed.

items.title: Literature audit
items.text: This audit informed the 0.1.0 design. Publication labels are conservative: the listed venue papers are peer reviewed; arXiv-only records are preprints unless a venue is named. Sources dated 2026 were supplied in the project brief and require bibliographic revalidation before scholarly publication.

items.title: Learned optimization
items.text:
Andrychowicz et al. (NeurIPS 2016) demonstrated coordinatewise recurrent optimizers trained by unrolling. Wichrowska et al. (ICML 2017) added hierarchical structure and broader tasks. Chen et al.'s JMLR 2022 survey formalized evaluation concerns and the gap between task-distribution success and general-purpose claims. VeLO (Metz et al., 2022 preprint) showed the value—and very large compute cost—of scale. Gärtner et al. (CVPR 2023) directly motivates attention over optimization trajectories. The NeurIPS 2022 universal hyperparameter-optimizer work uses transformers for transferable sequential decisions. B2Opt (AAAI 2025) addresses small-budget black-box search; MetaBox-v2 (2025 preprint) supplies an evolutionary-optimization benchmark ecosystem. The supplied 2026 gradient-history and Celo2 preprints are relevant recent claims, but their October 2026/arXiv and February 2026 status should be checked against canonical records before citation.

Common findings are sensitivity to training distributions, horizon truncation, feature normalization, meta-training cost, and incomplete comparisons after accounting for objective calls and wall time. Learned optimizers can exploit distributions; No Free Lunch results rule out uniform dominance over all objectives.

items.title: Representations and theory
items.text: Deep Sets establishes permutation-invariant set aggregation; Set Transformers add attention-based interactions. Von Oswald et al. (ICML 2023) construct transformer mechanisms that implement gradient-descent-like in-context updates, but this does not show that an arbitrary trained transformer discovers a robust numerical optimizer. Variable-cardinality attention, latent task tokens, coordinate permutations, normalized dimensionless features, and low-rank curvature representations are therefore useful inductive biases rather than guarantees. Bilevel unrolling provides gradients through training trajectories but creates truncation bias and memory cost. Generalization across dimension, horizon, rotations, and conditioning must be measured separately.

items.title: Certification
items.text:
Classical interval branch-and-bound derives admissible regional lower bounds, feasible upper bounds, and prunes only by proof. Natural interval extensions suffer dependency overestimation; centered forms, interval gradients/Hessians, interval Newton/Krawczyk operators, McCormick relaxations, and Taylor models can tighten bounds. IEEE 1788 specifies interval semantics and decorations; ordinary JAX/XLA arithmetic does not provide directed rounding. jax_verify propagates certified relaxations mainly for neural-network verification. jaxglobal explores JAX-oriented global optimization. Neither makes arbitrary JAX programs automatically certifiable. The supplied PNAS Nexus 2026 GPU interval-global-optimization DOI should be authenticated before its results are quoted.

The implemented backend consequently uses a tiny serializable expression subset and host binary64 nextafter expansion. It fails closed for arbitrary JAX programs. This is more limited than JAXPR interval interpretation, interval Newton, or a conforming IEEE 1788 library, but its claim is inspectable.

items.title: Evaluation
items.text: COCO/BBOB provides target-based, multi-instance benchmarking and discourages conclusions from a few analytic functions. bbob-jax helps batch/JIT evaluation, while MetaBox-v2 focuses learned evolutionary optimizers. Google learned_optimization provides tasks and learned-optimizer research infrastructure rather than a drop-in universally superior baseline. Sound studies need held-out families and instances, matched evaluation budgets, compile-time separation, paired seeds, confidence intervals, failures, and training cost.

items.title: Novelty and falsification
items.text:
The individual ingredients—transformers, learned updates, diagonal-plus-low-rank matrices, JAX, and interval branch-and-bound—are established. The candidate contribution is a compact experimental interface in which the same policy emits numerical updates and admissible search-order suggestions while certificate validity remains fully independent. This integration is a hypothesis, not established novelty or improved performance.

System family Learned direct update Variable dimension Native rigorous global bound Neural guidance can affect proof validity Evidence available here L2L / scalable recurrent optimizers Yes Varies No N/A Published studies Transformer learned optimizers Yes Varies No N/A Published studies B2Opt / MetaBox learned black-box methods Yes Often No N/A External studies SciPy/JAXopt/Optimistix No Yes No N/A Mature software Interval global solvers / jaxglobal No Yes Yes within subset N/A External software neuralopt 0.1.0 Yes Yes Yes under documented restricted assumptions No Local tests and demo only

Reported gaps in prior work include distribution shift, meta-training cost, weak wall-time accounting, unavailable weights, limited dimension/horizon transfer, and no rigorous relation between policy confidence and correctness. This package does not yet resolve them.

H1 is falsified if a trained checkpoint fails to beat its random initialization on held-out families and dimensions under paired budgets. H2 is falsified if matched SciPy and learned baselines dominate objective quality and time across the prespecified task distribution. H3 is falsified if learned ordering does not reduce median processed nodes at the same certified gap; correctness must be identical either way. H4 is falsified if inference overhead or instability erases evaluation savings, or parameter count/compute is not competitive. Gate thresholds for a larger study are: at least 20 held-out instances per family, five seeds, median regret improvement of 10% with a bootstrap 95% interval excluding zero for the claimed distribution, no increase in failure rate, and certificate replay success in every certified run.

items.title: Gate status
items.text:
• A — theory/dependencies: pass for native equations and dependency audit. Diffrax is optional; Exponax is deferred for lack of a justified PDE use.
  • B — overdamped Langevin: pass for fixed/episode-frozen geometry and numerical tests; optimization evidence is negative overall.
  • C — learned geometry: partial. Existing learned geometry executes, but no Langevin-specific checkpoint exists and identity is competitive or better.
  • D — underdamped dynamics: pass for fixed-mass BAOAB numerics and smoke comparison; learned-mass superiority is unsupported.
  • E — distribution-aware training: partial. Exact divergence, weak generator, and Gaussian free energy exist; transformer training ablations are unimplemented.
  • F — function space: partial. Periodic reference geometry refines correctly; learned cross-resolution transfer is untested.
  • G — certification: blocked. Stochastic incumbent injection is not integrated; certification and replay remain unchanged and passing.
  • H — repository validation: pending the final v0.3 validation pass.
path: Stochastic research limitations and gate record

items.title: Mathematical limitations
items.text:
Euler–Maruyama and BAOAB are biased at finite step size. The bounded logistic map excludes exact boundary states from stochastic dynamics, although the incumbent archive preserves boundary optima. Exact mobility divergence scales poorly with dimension. Weak residuals use Monte Carlo estimates and finite-time differences. History-adaptive transformer geometry has no fixed invariant target.

The function-space module validates a discretized reference problem, not an infinite-dimensional learned optimizer. No mesh-independent transformer claim, global convergence claim, or stochastic certification claim is supported.

The smoke study is too small for publication-level confidence intervals and its hyperparameters are not tuned on a separate validation distribution. All new stochastic methods remain opt-in.
path: Stochastic research limitations and gate record

items.title: Stochastic learned-geometry research status
items.text:
The research gap under investigation is narrower than “neural stochastic optimization.” Learned optimizers already predict updates and preconditioners; Riemannian Langevin/HMC and L2HMC already adapt sampling geometry. NeuralOpt asks whether a variable-dimensional transformer can transfer episode-frozen geometry across optimization task families while distributional structure regularizes candidate generation.

No novelty claim is established by the current implementation. The existing v0.1 transformer was not trained for Langevin mobility, and smoke results show that its geometry often underperforms identity. Exact divergence and weak-form utilities create a testable path to Fokker–Planck-informed training, but no such training ablation has yet demonstrated improved regret.

items.title: v0.3 smoke evidence
items.text:
The 15-instance, three-seed artifact is results/stochastic-smoke-v0.3.0.json. All variants use a nominal objective-call budget of 100 and report gradient/integration counts separately.

Variant Median objective Improvement rate Incumbent rate Warm time Direct 2.912 1.01% 1.01% 0.235 s Identity HMC 2.449 50.0% 31.25% 0.103 s Learned HMC 2.302 56.25% 18.75% 0.090 s Identity overdamped 7.986 51.52% 3.03% 0.135 s Learned overdamped 17.449 54.55% 3.03% 0.139 s Identity BAOAB 1.970 52.63% 15.79% 0.119 s Learned BAOAB 1.937 52.63% 21.05% 0.109 s

Overdamped identity and learned mobility beat direct on only 5/15 and 4/15 paired cases. Identity and learned BAOAB each beat direct on 11/15. Learned geometry has not established a consistent advantage over identity. Pooled objectives across different families are descriptive only, not a valid absolute accuracy statistic.

items.title: Mathematical specification
items.text:
At step t, normalized coordinate tokens contain the current point, incumbent, scaled gradient, gradient magnitude, and availability mask. Two learned task tokens aggregate the variable-cardinality sequence. Multi-head self-attention produces coordinate states. Heads emit direction d, independent proposal q, step alpha, positive diagonal D = softplus(z)+1e-4, and low-rank U. The update is

\[x_{t+1}=\Pi_{[l,u]}(x_t+\alpha(Dd+U(U^Td))).\]

The implementation never forms the dense preconditioner. Its strict positive diagonal makes D + UUᵀ positive definite, although the learned direction does not guarantee descent. Independently evaluated proposals alternate with update candidates. A fixed reject-and-contract rule prevents propagation of worse or nonfinite candidates.

Certification uses natural interval extensions with one-ULP outward expansion after every supported operation. Branch-and-bound preserves the domain by bisection, evaluates midpoint incumbents as point intervals, and prunes only if the interval lower bound is no smaller than the feasible upper bound. Termination requires U - min_R L(R) <= epsilon. The serialized certificate retains every terminal box, including pruned boxes. Verification re-evaluates their bounds, rejects overlapping interiors, and checks exact binary-rational volume equality with the declared domain before accepting the global gap.

Assumptions: IEEE-754 binary64, correctly rounded basic NumPy operations and elementary functions supplied by the platform libm, deterministic expression semantics, compact finite boxes, and no NaNs. Since IEEE 1788 decoration and a formally verified libm are absent, certificates are validated numerical results under these assumptions, not machine-checked formal proofs.

items.title: Outcome-driven training
items.text:
unrolled_regret_loss uses jax.lax.scan to differentiate projected learned updates. At configured horizons it minimizes robust normalized best-so-far regret, log1p(max(f_best-f*, 0) / max(|f_initial-f*|, 1)). It also includes small step, ascent-direction, and log-diagonal regularizers. There is no claimed gradient through hard inference acceptance or certified branching. Regret training requires an explicit problem.metadata["known_optimum"]; it never assumes that an untranslated objective has optimum zero. All differentiable normalizations use square-root smoothing so their derivatives remain finite at stationary points. Directional regularization transforms physical gradients into normalized box coordinates before comparing them with the learned direction, so anisotropic parameter widths cannot reverse the ascent/descent label. The imitation target uses the same normalized-coordinate gradient; no training objective now compares policy directions with gradients from a different coordinate system.

Training uses explicit PRNG keys, Optax global-norm clipping, nonfinite loss detection, and portable checkpoints. The test suite verifies finite, nonzero meta-gradients.

The first CPU smoke run used 12 meta-updates, 10 unrolled steps, horizons ⅖/10, and dimensions 2 and 4. It took 39.69 seconds. Loss rose from 0.2901 to 0.7010, and the checkpoint worsened an unseen 8D rotated quadratic from 89.41 to 164.71. The artifact is retained as neuralopt-v0.2.0-smoke.npz but is not promoted or bundled. This rejects the hypothesis that this tiny training budget is sufficient; validation-based early stopping and a substantially larger, family-separated curriculum remain required.

Per-task loss-and-gradient functions are now JIT compiled. Repeating the same 12-update, eight-task smoke configuration reduced training time from 39.69 to 21.10 seconds; a 20-update single-task run took 2.39 seconds. The remaining cost is dominated by first-use compilation for every distinct objective closure. Once compiled, a 10-step meta-gradient evaluation drops from about 1.69 seconds in eager mode to roughly 1.3 milliseconds on the same task. Grouping compatible tasks into batched, parameterized objective families is the principal training throughput opportunity.

items.title: Stochastic geometry training
items.text:
stochastic_geometry_loss differentiates through explicit-noise overdamped Euler or fixed-mass BAOAB trajectories. At every episode the transformer sees the current point, gradient, incumbent, and remaining budget, predicts a strictly positive diagonal plus low-rank factor, and freezes it for the episode. The next episode may predict different geometry, so the complete training policy is adaptive and has no fixed Gibbs invariant-measure guarantee. BAOAB training initializes momentum from N(0, T M) using the first predicted mass, matching inference and retaining the pathwise mass/noise gradient.

The primary loss is weighted multi-horizon log1p best-feasible regret. A normalized displacement penalty discourages unstable trajectories. Integration length is static, so the explicit objective/gradient compute term is constant and deliberately has zero parameter gradient; there is no differentiable early stopping surrogate. Best-so-far minimum and incumbent selection are nondifferentiable at ties and use JAX subgradients. Hard inference validity checks, certification branches, and benchmark timing do not lie on the training gradient path.

For overdamped training, a quadratic test function estimates the conditional weak generator identity for each episode-frozen mobility. Its Gaussian noise contribution is integrated analytically; sampling its square would add variance that spuriously rewards collapsing the mobility. The squared residual is passed through log1p before weighting because raw residual scales differ by orders of magnitude across task families. This checks the implemented Euler generator; it neither removes finite-step bias nor makes the history-adaptive policy stationary. The optional entropy term fits a Gaussian to trajectory states and is explicitly a free-energy surrogate, not exact differential entropy or thermodynamic free energy. It was disabled in the v0.4 reported experiment, and its dense covariance/log-determinant path is skipped completely when disabled.

The reproducible configuration and checkpoints are described in distribution-aware-training.md.

items.title: Trajectory diagnostics
items.text: The v0.2 diagnostic mode records one row per objective evaluation and does not perform extra objective calls. It distinguishes raw, preconditioned, projected, and accepted directions; objective and incumbent state; projection; boundary saturation; and exact small-dimensional preconditioner eigenvalues. Raw and preconditioned directions are compared with gradients transformed into normalized box coordinates. Applied physical displacements are compared with physical gradients, preventing unequal parameter widths from reversing reported ascent and descent.

items.title: Reproduction and dominant failure
items.text:
uv run python scripts/run_research_smoke.py reproduces the published trained median on the original held-out split (13.0525). The random-weight value is not reproducible because v0.1.0 did not record its seed. With seed 123 its median is 27.4117 rather than 195.745. The original files and checkpoint remain unchanged.

On six single-instance, four-dimensional smoke tasks (49 proposals after the initial evaluation), the trained raw direction has median descent cosine 0.833 on the isotropic quadratic and 0.994--0.999 on the other five tasks. Preconditioning changes this little and has median condition number 1.1--1.4. Nevertheless, acceptance is 0% on four tasks and 4.1% on the other two. The independent proposal head consumes 24/49 evaluations and accepts none.

This evidence rejects bad direction and ill-conditioned preconditioning as the dominant explanation in this sample. The primary failures are excessive step length, an unsupervised proposal head, and poor budget allocation. A separate implementation defect compounded this: rejection moved x without evaluating the new point, leaving its stored value inconsistent with its gradient. v0.2 leaves the current state unchanged after rejection.

The full machine-readable record is results/research-smoke-v0.2.0.json. This is a diagnostic smoke study, not an independent statistical benchmark.
